phonemes.desc: Short alpha — the name begins with an open, welcoming sound.
Aspirated phi plus rho, the breathy center that carries the name forward.
Delta plus acute on short iota — the pitched peak, bright and sharp.
Long eta, the final syllable that sustains and resolves.

pronunciation.approximation: 'ah-fro-DEE-tay' — the third syllable carries the pitch, and the final vowel is long and clear.

pronunciation.note: Aphrodítē is Tier 1 because the Greek Ἀφροδίτη contains both stress (acute on the short iota) and length (long η in the final syllable). The name's foam etymology makes the long final vowel sound like a wave receding.

domains.title: She Who Was Born of Foam
domains.subtitle: Love, Beauty, Desire, and Fertility
domains.lead: Aphrodítē is the goddess of desire in all its forms: sexual love, beauty, fertility, and the longing that binds mortals and gods. She is not a youthful virgin but a sovereign power who can make Zeús himself fall in love against his will.

cards.name: Sexual Desire
cards.desc: The force that overwhelms reason and unites bodies, whether in marriage or adultery.

cards.name: Beauty
cards.desc: The visible form of desire; her presence makes the ordinary radiant.

cards.name: Fertility and Generation
cards.desc: She guarantees the continuity of life through sexual union and the growth of crops.

cards.name: Divine Power
cards.desc: Even gods and heroes submit to her; no one is immune to desire.

mythology.lead: Aphrodítē's myths anatomize desire as a cosmic power — foam-born from an act of violence, sovereign over gods and mortals alike, equally capable of granting a prince his heart's wish, destroying the greatest city of the age, and making a faithful wife's ruin a matter of divine policy.

myths.title: Born from the Sea
myths.text: The Theogony (176–206) makes desire the child of violence. When Kronos castrated his father Ouranos and hurled the severed genitals into the sea, white foam (aphros) gathered around them, and from it a maiden grew, carried first to holy Cythera, then to sea-girt Cyprus, where she stepped ashore and grass flowered beneath her feet. Eros and fair Himeros walked with her as she went among the gods, and from the beginning she received her portion: ‘bribery of maidens’ whisperings and smiles and deceits, with which she delights the hearts of all.’ Hesiod names the foam deliberately, so the etymology is heard: Aphrodítē is the thing born from the most ephemeral substance in the world. The myth fuses brutality and beauty in a single image — love arriving wounded, unclothed, and already sovereign.

myths.title: The Apple of Discord
myths.text: At the wedding of Peleus and Thetis, every power was invited except Éris, who arrived anyway and rolled among the goddesses a golden apple marked tēi kallistēi — ‘for the fairest’ (Cypria, preserved in Proclus’ summary). Hēra, Athēnâ, and Aphrodítē claimed it, and the quarrel was sent for judgment to Paris on Mount Ida. Hēra offered empire, Athēnâ victory in war; Aphrodítē promised the most beautiful of mortal women — Helen of Sparta, though she was already another man’s wife. Paris chose desire, and the Cypria says flatly that from this judgment arose the Trojan War: the abduction, the thousand ships, ten years of siege, and the fall of a city older than memory. Lucian (Judgment of the Goddesses) later retells the scene as pure comedy; in Homer it is the engine of the Iliad’s whole world. The myth’s claim is structural: beauty, once made competitive, becomes catastrophe.

myths.title: Aphrodítē and Anchises
myths.text: The Homeric Hymn to Aphrodite (45–291) sends the goddess down to Mount Ida in the disguise of a mortal maiden to seduce the Trojan shepherd Anchises. Only afterward does she stand revealed in immortal stature and name the child she will bear — Aineias, Aeneas — who is to be reared by the mountain nymphs until he can be brought to his father. But the hymn ends in warning, not triumph: Anchises must never boast that he slept with the goddess, on pain of Zeús’s thunderbolt, and he grows old guarding the secret. Zeús had in fact engineered the whole affair to end Aphrodítē’s mockery of the other gods’ affairs with mortals by making her feel the same longing herself. The hymn’s theology is its point: desire is so much the goddess’s own nature that she alone among the gods is made to feel what mortals feel — longing, and its cost.

myths.title: Aphrodítē and Adonis
myths.text: The love of Aphrodítē and the beautiful hunter Adonis ends in annual mourning. The fullest account is Calliope’s song in Ovid’s Metamorphoses (10.298–559): Adonis’s mother Myrrha, cursed with love for her own father, became the myrrh tree, from whose bark the infant Adonis was born and entrusted to Aphrodítē. When the boy grew, both the goddess and Persephonē loved him; Zeús divided his year between them, and in the eighth month of Aphrodítē’s share a boar gored him. His blood became the anemone, a flower that fades as quickly as it opens. Sappho (fr. 140 LP) already knows the women’s ritual cry, and Lucian (On the Syrian Goddess 6) describes the great mourning at Byblos, where the river ran red with ‘Adonis’s blood’ each summer and women shaved their heads for him. The myth gives desire a calendar: what is loved most beautifully is lost most regularly.

myths.title: The Punishment of Hippolytus
myths.text: In Euripides’ Hippolytus, the young prince of Troezen dedicates himself wholly to Artemis and refuses Aphrodítē, boasting of his purity. The goddess answers with her oldest weapon: she fills his stepmother Phaedra with a forbidden passion for him. Ashamed and desperate, Phaedra hangs herself, leaving a letter that accuses Hippolytus of rape; Theseus, believing it, curses his own son, and Poseidôn sends a bull from the sea that shatters Hippolytus’s chariot against the rocks. The dying prince is carried back to his father by Artemis, who can do nothing but reveal the truth. Euripides gives the goddess the play’s opening and closing speeches without apology: mortals who will not honor love must be broken by it. The tragedy warns that desire cannot be legislated out of existence — denial invites its most destructive disguises.

lore.syncretism: The Romans identified Aphrodítē with Venus, originally a goddess of gardens and spring whose cult became one of the most powerful in Rome. Julius Caesar claimed descent from Venus through Aeneas, making her the divine ancestress of the Roman people. In the Renaissance she became the supreme subject of painting — Botticelli's 'Birth of Venus' is perhaps the most famous image of a pagan goddess in Western art. The planet Venus and the concept of 'venereal' preserve her name. Modern culture still uses her as the archetype of beauty and desire.
lore.culturalLegacy: Aphrodítē shaped Greek culture more deeply than any martial god. Marriage, prostitution, homosexual love, and civic festivals all fell under her patronage. The Aphrodisia was celebrated across the Greek world; her temples at Corinth and Cyprus were famous. In philosophy and poetry she became the symbol of erôs, the force that draws all things toward beauty and unity. The modern cosmetics and fashion industries are secular continuations of her cult. Restoring Aphrodítē with its full Greek accents restores the original sound of the goddess who rules desire itself.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Aphrodítē is the only Olympian whose power no one can refuse. Wisdom, strength, and even fate can be contested; desire simply arrives. The Greeks did not moralize this. They made her beautiful, dangerous, and sovereign. Her myths show that love can create harmony or ruin cities, and usually both.

In a digital age, desire is more engineered than ever — algorithms optimize for engagement, which often means optimizing for arousal. Aphrodítē's ancient dignity reminds us that desire is not merely a mechanism to be exploited. It is one of the fundamental forces of human life, and it deserves its original name.
lore.archaeology: Sanctuary of Aphrodite at Palaepaphos (Kouklia, Cyprus): a 12th-century BCE shrine with later ashlar temple, altar courts, and the famous Cypriot syllabary dedication 'Aphrodite's sanctuary.' At Cythera, the sanctuary of Aphrodite Ourania overlooked the sea from the sixth century BCE. Corinth's temple of Aphrodite on Acrocorinth is attested by Pausanias and excavation. The Knidia of Praxiteles (Roman copies, e.g., Vatican Museums) was housed in a circular tholos at Cnidus.
lore.cult: Aphrodítē’s cults ranged from the aniconic to the notorious. At Palaepaphos, her oldest home, there stood no statue at all but a conical stone — the goddess as baetyl — and Tacitus marveled that the shrine’s altar stayed dry in the rain; Strabo names the Cinyradae, hereditary priest-kings who served the Paphian goddess. The calendar kept her everywhere: the Aphrodisia in Greek cities each summer, and the Adonia, when women raised ‘gardens of Adonis’ on rooftops and mourned the dead lover — Theocritus paints the Alexandrian version. Corinth’s temple on Acrocorinth was famous for hetairai consecrated to the goddess, a practice to which Pindar’s fragment on Xenophon’s hundred-girl vow and Strabo’s thousand testify, whatever scholars now say about the literal accounting. Votive terracottas by the thousand, perfume jars, and mirrors mark her sanctuaries’ debris: worship here was beauty’s economy, offerings and flowers circulating through one temple gate.
lore.iconography: She entered art draped and left it naked. Archaic vase-painters show a fully clothed goddess attended by Eros and birds — a woman in fine linen, remarkable chiefly for the goose or swan at her side. The earliest monumental statement of her birth is the Ludovisi Throne relief (c. 460 BCE, Museo Nazionale Romano, Palazzo Altemps), whose central panel is generally read as the goddess rising from the foam, two winged attendants lifting her. Then, around 350 BCE, Praxiteles exhibited at Cnidus the first monumental female nude in Greek art — Aphrodite lifting her garment before the bath — and copies at the Vatican record the type; the scandal, and the pilgrims, were a cultural event in themselves. Hellenistic taste multiplied bathing and crouching variants, and the Venus de Milo (Louvre, c. 150–100 BCE) fixed the Western canon. Dove, sparrow, swan, and later the scallop shell remain her constants — the attributes by which any museum visitor picks her out today.
lore.reception: Antiquity closed over her slowly: the Paphian cult was still living in the fourth century CE, and Christian emperors legislated against her festivals while her stones stayed standing. The Middle Ages received her mainly through Ovid — the Heroides and the Ars amatoria copied in every cathedral school, and in fourteenth-century France re-imagined as the Ovide moralisé, where Venus was allegorized into doctrine. The Renaissance made the anadyomene pose painting’s most licensed subject, and early modern galleries filled with pudica Venuses. Three events fixed her modern image: Winckelmann’s History of Ancient Art (1764), which made Greek sculpture the measure of beauty and her statues its evidence; the discovery of the Venus de Milo on Melos in 1820 and her immediate installation in the Louvre; and the Cesnola excavations at Palaepaphos (1865–71), which carried her original sanctuary to the Metropolitan Museum. Philology kept pace: the question Herodotus raised (1.105: is Ourania the Aštart of Ascalon?) became the modern debate over her eastern origin, still argued from Orientalizing Revolution onward. Her name survives chemically, in ‘aphrodisiac’ — a transmission no cult could have planned.
